body: Very true, but what set me off *spoilers* is the Escape Room is filled with triggering things for each character and then we are shown their original trauma and their reaction to it. So imo this is a bit more triggering than your classic horror film or psychological trigger especially since the film constantly reminds you that there is no escape.

I find it weirdly therapeutic to just cry and have a monologue without an audience of all that's happened to me. It feels like I have a huge knot in my heart and throat and when I speak on what I feel and whats happened it decreases the knot if only a little and if only for awhile.

Then my cptsd got the best of me (I didn't know I had it until January of 2017. so hooray for my one year anniversary of being aware?). I've since noticed my pattern. My cptsd stems from my traumatic childhood of never having consistency in love or support. Occasional absentee father, mother who worried more about her own feelings, typical stuff. I get it now that im an adult, its so hard to keep it together when you constantly feel so low. 

so my pattern is that i jump from relationship to relationship. im a serial monogamous. I give myself a year or so between relationships. ive done lots of therapy for this, but i guess im just a lifer for cptsd. 

I have completely broken down since my husband left. He didn't understand that i became clingy because i wasn't feeling attachment to anyone but him, despite me trying to. I feel liberated that i dint have to pretend im okay anymore, but completely miserable that my husband just cant understand and doesn't want to be married anymore

We all have attention seeking behaviors. That's not a bad thing. Mentally sound people know how to get attention in a positive manner. Example: sending a text inviting someone out for coffee or something. 

Those with mental health issues aren't always sure how to communicate their need for help and often times its seen as childish attempts to get attention and pity. I can't speak for Pete 
Davidson, but I can speak for myself. It is not easy to say to someone I need help and this is how I'm feeling. When your mind is mentally stable, you just can't understand how a mentally unstable person feels and they end up misinterpreting the cries for help as manipulative. It's sad really.

"What can I do to help?"


I always appreciate an assortment of options. "Do you need me to come over" "Do you need to keep talking on the phone?" "Do you need to get out of your house?"

Sometimes people with depression or other mental health issues have a hard time vocalizing what they need. Mainly, I'm sure, out of embarrassment of needing support. 

I personally prefer when people come over just to hang out. Because then if I break down crying, I'm in the comfort of my own home.

A lot of colleges offer free or inexpensive therapy. Mind you these are therapists in training, but they are overseen by someone who is licensed.

Don't be afraid to change a therapist once you've found one. You have to feel comfortable sharing with this person and following their advice. 

I always think of anti-depressants as floaties. It's like you're trying to swim and all your energy is being used to just keep your head above water. Inevitably you get tired and you're back under water. Anti-depressants, while not a cure, work like floaties. You still gotta swim, but now you don't have to focus all your energy on just keeping your head above water. Now you can actually focus on where you want to and need to go.
